A Jev engineer hasn’t waited on a CI pipeline in three months, and his changes still reach production faster and safer than the rest of the team’s

He never sped the pipeline up. He routed around it, letting every change prove itself on live traffic users never see.

> SHADOW - each change runs beside production on a mirrored copy of real traffic
> JUDGE - the Jev system compares both outputs request by request, never by averages
> SWAP - a change that matches or beats live behaviour goes in, with a 200 ms rollback armed

CI was built for a world where real traffic was too risky to touch, so it tests against guesses about what users do.

Shadow traffic removes the guess. The new code sees exactly what users send, and its answers simply never reach them.

The comparison is the hard part. Two outputs can differ and both be right, so Jev scores intent instead of exact matches.

Most changes clear in minutes. The ones that fail get caught on the exact request that broke them, input attached.

The armed rollback is what makes it safe. One bad response and the old path is back before the next request lands.

His team still writes tests. They just stopped treating a green checkmark as proof that real users will be fine.

His full setup, from the traffic mirror to the rollback trigger, is written up in the article attached here.

Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 built the same gearbox. On screen, a tie. On the print bed, one of them came out as a single fused brick.

Fable is the pricier model and works through every detail. Opus costs less and builds exactly what was asked, nothing more.

> SPEC - one gearbox described in a paragraph: housing, shafts, three meshing gears
> SOLID - each model outputs the parts as separate watertight bodies, ready to export
> SLICE - both files pushed through the same slicer profile with no manual fixes
> PRINT - the whole gearbox printed in place as one job, identical filament and heat
> TURN - the finished assembly driven by hand to see whether anything actually spins

On the monitor the two gearboxes looked interchangeable. Teeth meshed, shafts lined up, nothing intersected.

Opus 5.5 modelled every part exactly to size. Exact is the problem: printed plastic swells, and a zero gap becomes a weld.

Its gearbox came off the bed as one solid block. Every gear was there, perfectly shaped, and none of them could turn.

Fable 5.1 left roughly 0.3 mm of air around each moving face without being told to. Its gearbox spun on the first try.

It also chamfered the bottom edges and split the housing so the gears can be serviced later. Neither was in the brief.

One model built the drawing. The other built the object the drawing is supposed to become.

Opus is the cheaper pick for drafts and blockouts. Fable’s 2.5x premium pays for that 0.3 mm and everything around it.

A render forgives everything. A printer forgives nothing, and it never grades on a curve.

The two files, the slicer profile and the clearance each model picked are packed into the thread.

Anthropic turned one GitHub request into a living 3D model that answers every new issue with a rebuilt version of itself

Opus 5.5 builds the whole system from that first request, from geometry and rig to the viewer and the pipeline behind it.

> REQUEST - one issue describes the object in plain words, nothing else needed
> BUILD - mesh, rig and materials generated and committed as editable source files
> VIEW - a browser viewer added to the repo so anyone can spin the model instantly
> LISTEN - every new issue is read as a change request against the current model
> PATCH - only what changed gets rebuilt, then a pull request opens with a fresh render

A 3D asset is normally a dead file. Someone exports it once, and every later change means opening the software again.

Here the model stays alive inside the repo. Ask for a longer handle or a softer material, and it answers in a pull request.

Each pull request carries a new render, so the change gets reviewed by eye before anyone merges it.

Because the source is code and not a binary blob, every version is diffable. You see exactly which part moved and why.

Rejected changes cost nothing. Close the pull request and the model stays exactly as it was.

Teams already run software this way. Running a 3D model like a codebase is the part nobody had wired up.

The first request, the repo layout and one full issue-to-render cycle are pinned in the article.

▸ https://t.co/jS5B97QbWp

WORKERS CAN’T TOUCH REAL SYSTEMS

the architecture from the video is the part worth understanding

Opus handles difficult decisions and architecture

Sonnet coordinates implementation and task execution

Haiku handles smaller focused jobs like exploration and research

workers return their findings to the higher reasoning layer for review

the trick is not spawning 20 agents and hoping they cooperate

it’s matching task complexity to model cost, isolating context and verifying the result before the next task begins

one expensive model doing everything is a terrible default when you can build an entire execution tree around it

4 routines worth stealing:

1.⁠ ⁠Find real AI workflows  
Filters X for actual workflows with a clear task, tool and measurable result, while skipping hype threads and product launches.

Prompt:
“Every weekday at 9:15am in my time zone, search X and the web for new AI workflows people are actually running. Keep only cases that name the old task, the tool, and the result: time saved, a step removed, or a handoff that used to need a person. Drop product announcements, ‘10 prompts’ threads, and anything the author has not used more than once. Return at most 3. For each, give the link, the job it replaces, what I would need connected, and whether it fits my work. Send it to me on Slack. Do not post or reply anywhere else. Save this as a routine. If nothing qualifies, send one line saying so.”

2.⁠ ⁠Catch every brand mention  
Finds mentions, labels sentiment, and sends the team a clean Slack digest.

Prompt:
“Every weekday at 9:00am, search X for mentions in the last 24 hours of [your brand, @handle, or your own name]. For each hit, give the author, link, a one-line summary, and whether it is praise, complaint, question, or neutral. Do not reply to anyone. Post the digest in [your Slack channel] and tag me. Save this as a routine. If a source is unavailable, say which one.”

3.⁠ ⁠Find people actively looking for what you sell  
Monitors X for reviews, comparison requests, and pain points around your category.

Prompt:
“Every 4 hours, search X for people evaluating [your category]. Catch three things: reviews or complaints about [category]; posts asking which [category] to use; and complaints about the problem [your product] solves. Quote the post, link it, name the account, and label it review, shopping, or complaint. Skip anything older than 24 hours, and skip [category] accounts promoting themselves. Post to [your Slack channel] only if there is at least one new hit you haven’t already shared. Do not reply to or interact with anyone. Save this as a routine. If the search fails, report the failure in Slack.”

4.⁠ ⁠Never lose a new contact  
Checks recent contacts and turns them into follow-up tasks without messaging anyone automatically.

Prompt:
“Every weekday at 8:30am in my time zone, read my address book and list contacts added in the last 14 days. For each, show name, date added, phone, email, and any note. Ask me what we talked about before you write anything. Once I reply, draft a follow-up task for each person in [your task tool] with the context attached. Never text, email, or call anyone. Save this as a routine. If the address book is unavailable, say so and do not use old data.”

These are way more useful than just asking a bot questions manually.

THE PLAN FALLS APART

→ turns vague coding requests into implementation plans with testing and review checkpoints

05 anthropics/skills
▸ https://t.co/jS5B97QbWp

WORKERS CAN’T TOUCH REAL SYSTEMS

06 modelcontextprotocol/servers
▸ https://t.co/pBf32aGMfP
→ reference MCP servers for connecting agents to external tools and data

07 anthropics/claude-code-action
▸ https://t.co/jv2p0wPns0
→ runs Claude Code inside GitHub Actions so repository workflows can trigger coding tasks

NOBODY KNOWS WHAT THE AGENTS DID

▸ https://t.co/HqjNuZo4I1

the architecture from the video is the part worth understanding

Opus handles difficult decisions and architecture

Sonnet coordinates implementation and task execution

Haiku handles smaller focused jobs like exploration and research

workers return their findings to the higher reasoning layer for review

the trick is not spawning 20 agents and hoping they cooperate

it’s matching task complexity to model cost, isolating context and verifying the result before the next task begins

one expensive model doing everything is a terrible default when you can build an entire execution tree around it

outsiders.text:
Opus 5.5 + Jev: 10 GitHub repos where Jev makes every call and your agents just do the work

opus writes the code. Jev answers the small questions in between: which model, which chunk, which click, is it really done. code enforces the answer.

1. jev-ultrafast
▸ https://t.co/wvXRnng6El
→ a browser agent from Browser Use: Jev picks the action and the exact DOM element in one round trip, a small LLM only types the text. Zürich → London on Google Flights in 7.1s

2. mu
▸ https://t.co/xdGBMgPeBh
→ a Pi-based coding agent where Jev answers at 38 decision points, like which chunks of a tool output ever reach the context. on their own test logs it cut 40% and lost 0 of 72 required lines

3. Jevonian
▸ https://t.co/1kBznCYkbl
→ a local OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible proxy for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex: one Jev call picks the model and the thinking level for every turn, a local ledger logs why

4. pi-warden
▸ https://t.co/dVywyoz9EM
→ watches your agent for rule breaks, risky actions, stuck loops and fake "done" claims. 1,168 real sessions: 419 risky actions held before they ran, 76% of fake "done"s turned into real test runs

5. Oko
▸ https://t.co/3ajuR3CXvK
→ Jev ranks which code snippets actually answer the agent's question, Oko serves only those over MCP. 60-63% fewer tokens in their Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode runs

6. jev-pref
▸ https://t.co/qTKSWGoyDE
→ write your project preferences once in jev-pref.json, Jev checks every diff against them and feeds the findings back to the agent. setup is one line: npx jev-pref setup

7. taste-lint
▸ https://t.co/jyrp7noj5C
→ catches AI slop in your UI, copy and agent instructions before it ships. 28 hard checks block the commit, the judgment calls go to Jev and come back with a probability

8. jev-review
▸ https://t.co/oI5e0W9p7q
→ a staged code review with a local dashboard: Jev picks the risky files, the evidence, the mechanism and the severity, code applies the thresholds

9. opencode-jev-orchestrator
▸ https://t.co/S0sMpUKpCw
→ the parent model stays fixed so the cache stays warm, Jev spots the hard turns and hands them to temporary subagents

10. yoshi
▸ https://t.co/UwWsDtWlKF
→ a Claude Code/Codex proxy where Jev decides which old tool output can leave the request, tool IDs and structure stay byte-identical. still a proof of concept and slower than baseline for now

same split in all 10:
> Opus does the work
> Jev makes the calls
> Code enforces them
